purpose: Enfortumab vedotin is used to treat a type of bladder cancer called urothelial cancer. It is used when the cancer has spread or cannot be removed by surgery, and other treatments have been tried. It can be used alone or combined with another cancer medicine called pembrolizumab.
how_it_works: Think of this medicine as a smart missile. It has two parts — an antibody that acts like a GPS, finding and attaching to cancer cells, and a powerful chemotherapy drug attached to it. Once it locks onto the cancer cell, it delivers the chemotherapy right inside the cell to destroy it, while trying to leave healthy cells alone.
common_side_effects: Tiredness and low energy, loss of appetite, hair loss, nausea, dry or itchy skin, rash, numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, changes in taste, constipation or diarrhea, and low blood sugar levels.
warnings: This medicine can cause serious skin reactions, including very bad rashes that can be life-threatening — tell your doctor right away if you develop a rash or blisters. It can also cause nerve damage in your hands and feet, eye problems such as dry or irritated eyes, high blood sugar, and serious lung problems. It may harm an unborn baby, so use reliable birth control during treatment and for some time after. Tell your doctor about all your medicines, as some can interact with this drug.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given through an IV (a drip into your vein) by a healthcare provider, usually once a week for 2 weeks in a row, followed by 1 week off — this 3-week period is called one cycle. The exact dose is based on your body weight. Your doctor will decide how many cycles you need based on how your body responds and how you tolerate the treatment.
